sources.ref_file_title: GL89 - A Hard-Core Predicate for All One-Way Functions

pages.class_justification: Left `unstated`: the hypothesis is a hardness assumption, not a primitive quantified over implementations, so the RTV04 notions are degenerate here, and every assumption-hypothesis edge in content/Reductions is left unstated. The hard-core-bit reduction (ACGS88, GL89) runs any CPA distinguisher as an oracle and touches the RSA function only through evaluation and trapdoor inversion.
pages.model_justification: No idealized oracle: the hard-core-bit construction and its reduction are standard-model.
pages.statement: The [[rsa-assumption|RSA assumption]] implies [[public-key-encryption|PKE]]. The scheme of [[RSA78 - A method for obtaining digital signatures and public-key cryptosystems|RSA78]], $\Enc(\pk, m) = m^e \bmod n$ and $\Dec(\sk, c) = c^d \bmod n$, is one-way under the RSA assumption but deterministic, hence not CPA-secure; CPA security for one-bit messages follows by encrypting $b$ as $(x^e \bmod n,\; b \oplus h(x))$ for $x \getsr \ZZ_n^*$ and a hard-core predicate $h$ of the RSA function — [[ACGS88 - RSA and Rabin Functions Certain Parts are as Hard as the Whole|ACGS88]], [[GL89 - A Hard-Core Predicate for All One-Way Functions|GL89]].
pages.sketch: The ciphertext $(x^e \bmod n,\, b \oplus h(x))$ hides $b$ exactly as well as $h(x)$ is unpredictable from $x^e \bmod n$; decryption recovers $x = y^d \bmod n$ with the trapdoor $d$. A CPA distinguisher is a predictor for $h$, which the hard-core reduction turns into an RSA inverter.
pages.improvements_text:
- The least-significant bit of the RSA function is hard-core: predicting it from $x^e \bmod n$ with advantage $1/\poly(\secpar)$ yields an RSA inverter — [[ACGS88 - RSA and Rabin Functions Certain Parts are as Hard as the Whole|ACGS88]].
- A hard-core predicate for every one-way function, giving the same bit encryption without an RSA-specific argument — [[GL89 - A Hard-Core Predicate for All One-Way Functions|GL89]].
flags: rsa-to-pke-rsa78: RSA78's own scheme is deterministic and not CPA-secure; the statement therefore names the hard-core-bit step. If the wiki reads `pke` as syntax plus one-wayness only, RSA78 alone suffices and ACGS88/GL89 can be dropped.

rsa-to-pke-rsa78: this edge is the composite of red-rsa-to-tdp-rsa78 and red-tdp-to-pke. Direct assumption-to-PKE edges are the repo norm (ddh-to-pke-elgamal85, lwe-to-pke-reg05, dcr-to-pke-pai99), so keeping it is consistent; a human may prefer the two-link path.

sources.ref_file_title: RSA78 - A method for obtaining digital signatures and public-key cryptosystems
sources.authors: Ronald L. Rivest, Adi Shamir, Leonard Adleman

sources.note: Existing reference page (cryptobib JC:GolRot13); abstract read from content/References.

pages.class_justification: Left `unstated`: the hypothesis is a hardness assumption, so the RTV04 notions are degenerate, and the repo leaves every assumption-hypothesis edge unstated. Here the construction is the RSA family itself and the reduction is the identity, so no class carries information.
pages.statement: The [[rsa-assumption|RSA assumption]] implies [[trapdoor-permutation|TDP]]: for $n = pq$ and $e$ coprime to $\varphi(n)$, $x \mapsto x^e \bmod n$ permutes $\ZZ_n^*$, the trapdoor $d$ with $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\varphi(n)}$ inverts it as $y \mapsto y^d \bmod n$, and one-wayness of this family is the RSA assumption — [[RSA78 - A method for obtaining digital signatures and public-key cryptosystems|RSA78]]. The domain is $\ZZ_n^*$ rather than $\bits^\ell$; applications that sample domain elements from public coins — [[oblivious-transfer|OT]], [[non-interactive-zero-knowledge|NIZK]] — need the enhanced or doubly enhanced notions — [[GR13 - Enhancements of Trapdoor Permutations|GR13]].
pages.improvements_text: - Enhanced and doubly enhanced trapdoor permutations, the notions the OT and NIZK applications require, are defined, compared, and shown to suffice for those applications — [[GR13 - Enhancements of Trapdoor Permutations|GR13]].
flags: HIGH -- rsa-to-tdp-rsa78: the migrated Statement carries two quotes that belong to other edges. The BFM88 bullet ('NIZK for all NP from trapdoor permutations ... in the CRS model') is the TDP + CRS => NIZK edge (red-tdp-to-nizk-bfm88, model: crs), and the 'which in turn imply PKE' tail is red-tdp-to-pke. Both should be dropped from this page; the single trailing RSA78 citation is misattributed to them.

HIGH -- rsa-to-tdp-rsa78: the same misattributed BFM88 parenthetical also produced content/Reductions/dlog-to-tdp.md ('DLOG => TDP', source: folklore), whose entire Statement is that parenthetical. No trapdoor permutation is known from the discrete logarithm assumption; that page (another batch) should be disposed wrong_claim.

rsa-to-tdp-rsa78: certifying that a claimed $(n, e)$ indexes a permutation is a further caveat that GR13's enhancement axis does not cover; left out of the statement rather than attached to an unverified citation.

rsa-to-tdp-rsa78: the statement does not claim that RSA satisfies the (doubly) enhanced notions; it only records that OT/NIZK need them. A human may add that claim with a citation (Goldreich, Foundations of Cryptography vol. 2, App. C, or GR13 §on RSA) if desired.

sources.ref_file_title: MM11b - Pseudorandom Knapsacks and the Sample Complexity of LWE Search-to-Decision Reductions
sources.note: cryptobib_key: C:MicMol11 (verified in vendor/cryptobib: CRYPTO 2011, pp. 465-484, DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-22792-9_26; eprint 2011/521). Key MM11 is taken in content/References by Matsuda-Matsuura, 'On Black-Box Separations among Injective One-Way Functions' (TCC 2011); suffixed per the collision rule. The sample-preserving claim was confirmed via search snippets of the abstract only.

pages.class_justification: Left `unstated`: the hypothesis is a hardness assumption, so the RTV04 notions are degenerate, and the repo leaves every assumption-hypothesis edge unstated. The reduction runs the decision distinguisher as an oracle.
pages.statement: If [[learning-with-errors#search-lwe|search LWE]] with parameters $(n, q, \chi)$ is hard for every polynomial number of samples, where $q$ is prime and $q = \poly(n)$, then [[learning-with-errors#decision-lwe|decision LWE]] with the same $(n, q, \chi)$ is hard for every polynomial number of samples: an efficient distinguisher between $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{A}\mathbf{s} + \mathbf{e})$ and $(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{u})$ using $m$ samples yields an efficient algorithm that recovers $\mathbf{s}$ from $\poly(n, m)$ samples — [[Reg05 - On Lattices, Learning with Errors, Random Linear Codes, and Cryptography|Reg05]].
pages.sketch: Recover $\mathbf{s}$ one coordinate at a time. To test the guess $\mathbf{s}_i = \ell$, map each sample $(\mathbf{a}, b)$ to $(\mathbf{a} + r\mathbf{u}_i,\; b + r\ell)$ for the $i$-th unit vector $\mathbf{u}_i$ and a fresh uniform $r \in \ZZ_q$: the new sample is $(\mathbf{a}', \langle \mathbf{a}', \mathbf{s}\rangle + e + r(\ell - \mathbf{s}_i))$, LWE-distributed when $\ell = \mathbf{s}_i$ and uniform otherwise, since $r(\ell - \mathbf{s}_i)$ is uniform for prime $q$. Running the distinguisher over all $nq$ pairs $(i, \ell)$ reads off $\mathbf{s}$, which is why $q$ must be polynomial; the random self-reduction $(\mathbf{a}, b) \mapsto (\mathbf{a}, b + \langle \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{t}\rangle)$ for uniform $\mathbf{t}$ first turns an average-case distinguisher into one that works for every $\mathbf{s}$.
pages.improvements_text: - Sample-preserving search-to-decision reductions: for a wide range of parameters, $m$ LWE samples are pseudorandom whenever search LWE is one-way for the same $m$ — [[MM11b - Pseudorandom Knapsacks and the Sample Complexity of LWE Search-to-Decision Reductions|MM11b]].
flags: HIGH -- search-lwe-to-decision-lwe: the migrated body proves the WRONG direction. Under the repo's orientation ('A => B' means 'A hard implies B hard', as fixed by cdh-to-dlog and ddh-to-cdh), this page is the hard direction — a decision distinguisher yields a search solver, Reg05 Lemma 4.2 — but the quoted text ('a search solver gives a decision adversary for free') proves red-decision-lwe-to-search-lwe. The two pages' Statement bodies are swapped: content/Reductions/decision-lwe-to-search-lwe.md currently carries the coordinate-by-coordinate Regev argument that belongs here. Fix both together.

search-lwe-to-decision-lwe: consequently the sibling red-decision-lwe-to-search-lwe is the EASY direction and is genuine folklore (run the search solver, accept iff $\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{A}\hat{\mathbf{s}}$ is short), conditional on $\chi$ being efficiently recognisable. Its batch owner should not source it to Reg05, and its migration note about the $O(qnm)$ sample count belongs on this page instead.
search-lwe-to-decision-lwe: kept as `implication`, not `equivalence` — both directions exist as separate pages.

pages.wrong_reason: Not a theorem. The wiki defines SK-PIR (content/Primitives/single-server-private-information-retrieval.md § Secret-Key PIR) as $o(N)$ online communication with no bound on server computation, 'contrast: SK-DEPIR, which requires both', and DEPIR (content/Primitives/doubly-efficient-pir.md) as $o(n)$ communication and $o(n)$ server computation per query. Storing the client's state encrypted on the server changes where the state lives, not how much work the server does. As a general implication the edge would give SK-DEPIR from one-way functions, via red-hash-function-to-secret-key-pir-sk-pir-bm26 and SKE from OWFs, which is open and conjectured impossible for black-box constructions (LMW25, already cited on doubly-efficient-pir.md). The migrated text is an editor's aside in the Notes of content/References/CIMR25 - Secret-Key PIR from Random Linear Codes.md ('But I could preprecess the database and store the state encrypted on the server'), specific to CIMR25's $O(s + n/s)$ construction; it is attributable to no paper, and downloading the encrypted state on every query costs $|\st|$ communication unless amortised, which the text does not address.

sources.ref_file_title: JDF11 - Towards quantum-resistant cryptosystems from supersingular elliptic curve isogenies
sources.note: Existing reference page (cryptobib PQCRYPTO:JaoDeF11, pp. 19-34). JDF11 prove session-key security in the Canetti-Krawczyk authenticated-links model under SSDDH, the decisional variant. Verifier: confirmed via search snippets (eprint blocked); secret scalars $m_A, n_A$ and kernel $[m]P + [n]Q$ likewise.

pages.class_justification: Left `unstated`: the hypothesis is a hardness assumption, so the RTV04 notions are degenerate, and the repo leaves every assumption-hypothesis edge unstated. The security proof is essentially the identity: session-key indistinguishability is SSDDH restated for the protocol transcript.
pages.model_justification: JDF11 prove session-key security in the Canetti-Krawczyk authenticated-links model under SSDDH, with no idealized oracle.
pages.statement: The [[supersingular-isogeny-diffie-hellman|SIDH]] assumption implies [[key-exchange|KE]]. Over a supersingular $E/\FF_{p^2}$ with $p = \ell_A^{e_A}\ell_B^{e_B} f \pm 1$, each party computes a secret isogeny with kernel $\langle [m]P + [n]Q \rangle$ for a basis $\{P, Q\}$ of its own $\ell^{e}$-torsion, publishes the image curve together with the images of the other party's torsion basis, and both derive $j(E_{AB})$; the session key is indistinguishable from random in the authenticated-links model of Canetti and Krawczyk under the decisional variant SSDDH — [[JDF11 - Towards quantum-resistant cryptosystems from supersingular elliptic curve isogenies|JDF11]]. The hypothesis is false: the published torsion images make the secret isogeny recoverable in classical polynomial time — [[CD22 - An efficient key recovery attack on SIDH|CD22]].
pages.sketch: Given $\phi_A(P_B), \phi_A(Q_B)$, Bob computes $E_A / \langle [m_B]\phi_A(P_B) + [n_B]\phi_A(Q_B) \rangle$, and Alice symmetrically; both curves are $E / \langle R_A, R_B \rangle$ up to isomorphism, so the $j$-invariants agree. Distinguishing $j(E_{AB})$ from the $j$-invariant of an independently generated $E_{A'B'}$ given the transcript is SSDDH by definition.
notes_to_keep: SUSPECTED ERROR on content/Assumptions/supersingular-isogeny-diffie-hellman.md: the shared-key line $j(E_{AB}) = j(\phi_B(E_A)) = j(\phi_A(E_B))$ applies each party's own isogeny to the other party's curve. The correct objects are the pushed-forward isogenies $\phi_B' : E_A \to E_{AB}$ and $\phi_A' : E_B \to E_{AB}$ computed from the transmitted torsion-point images; as written the composition is not defined.

SUSPECTED ERROR on the same page: the SIDH problem is stated with $E' = E/\langle P \rangle$ for a random $\ell$-torsion point $P$ while $\{P, Q\}$ is called a basis of the $\ell^n$-torsion. The kernel is $\langle [m]P + [n]Q \rangle$ for secret $m, n$, and both basis images of the other party's torsion group are published.
flags: sidh-to-ke-jdf11: .reductions/suspected-errors.json contains an entry whose affectsEdges lists red-sidh-to-ke-jdf11. Both suspected errors concern the assumption page's description of the protocol, not this edge's claim; the edge stays `sourced`. Kept in notes_to_keep.

sidh-to-ke-jdf11: the reduction remains valid while its hypothesis is false (CD22). The statement says so; CD22 already has a reference page.

VERIFIER -- sidh-to-ke-jdf11: prime form changed from '$p + 1 = \ell_A^{e_A}\ell_B^{e_B}$' to JDF11's '$p = \ell_A^{e_A}\ell_B^{e_B} f \pm 1$' (cofactor $f$), and the kernel from the later '$P + [s]Q$' normalisation to JDF11's '$[m]P + [n]Q$'. Abstract (via search snippets): 1-out-of-N OT from log N invocations of 1-out-of-2 OT, and as a direct corollary an efficient transformation of any PIR into SPIR without increasing the number of databases.

sources.ref_file_title: DMO00 - Single Database Private Information Retrieval Implies Oblivious Transfer
sources.authors: Giovanni Di Crescenzo, Tal Malkin, Rafail Ostrovsky
sources.note: Existing reference page (cryptobib EC:DiCMalOst00; also used by red-cpir-to-ot-dmo00). Its abstract identifies 1-out-of-n OT with SPIR ('a 1-out-of-n Oblivious Transfer protocol (also called SPIR)').

pages.class_justification: The construction is the identity: the SPIR protocol run on database $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ with query index $c$ is a $1$-out-of-$n$ OT, client privacy being receiver privacy and data privacy sender privacy. Each security reduction runs the OT adversary unchanged, as an oracle, against the corresponding SPIR property.
pages.statement: Single-server [[single-server-private-information-retrieval#symmetric-private-information-retrieval-single-server|symmetric PIR]] implies [[oblivious-transfer|OT]]: an SPIR protocol on database $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ with query index $c$ is a [[oblivious-transfer#k-out-of-n-ot|$1$-out-of-$n$ OT]] — client privacy is receiver privacy, data privacy is sender privacy — and $n = 2$ gives $1$-out-of-$2$ OT — folklore. The converse is not known: SPIR is $1$-out-of-$n$ OT with communication sublinear in $n$, no construction of sublinear-communication PIR from OT alone is known, and [[NP99 - Oblivious transfer and polynomial evaluation|NP99]] obtain SPIR from PIR plus $\log n$ OTs.
pages.improvements_text:
- Any single-server [[single-server-private-information-retrieval|PIR]] becomes SPIR with $\log n$ additional invocations of $1$-out-of-$2$ OT and no additional server — [[NP99 - Oblivious transfer and polynomial evaluation|NP99]].
- Non-trivial single-server PIR implies OT without any data-privacy requirement, and reduces communication-efficiently to $1$-out-of-$n$ OT — [[DMO00 - Single Database Private Information Retrieval Implies Oblivious Transfer|DMO00]].
flags: HIGH -- symmetric-private-information-retrieval-single-server-to-ot: `kind` must change from equivalence to implication. The page's own qualifier ('with an additional efficiency requirement') breaks the equivalence: SPIR => 1-out-of-n OT is immediate, but OT => SPIR would need sublinear-communication PIR from OT, which is not known (NP99 need a PIR plus log n OTs; DMO00 show the PIR hypothesis is the load-bearing one).

sources.ref_file_title: CHKP10 - Bonsai Trees, or How to Delegate a Lattice Basis
sources.authors: David Cash, Dennis Hofheinz, Eike Kiltz, Chris Peikert
sources.note: cryptobib_key: EC:CHKP10 (verified in vendor/cryptobib: EUROCRYPT 2010, pp. 523-552, DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-13190-5_27; journal JC:CHKP12 pp. 601-639; eprint 2010/591). Contribution used here: stateless hash-and-sign signatures from SIS in the standard model.

pages.class_justification: Left `unstated`: the hypothesis is a hardness assumption, so the RTV04 notions are degenerate, and the repo leaves every assumption-hypothesis edge unstated. The GPV08 reduction runs the forger as an oracle and programs the random oracle.
pages.model_justification: GPV08 prove the hash-and-sign scheme unforgeable in the random oracle model — the reduction programs $H$ by sampling the preimage first — so the current frontmatter value `standard` is wrong. A standard-model SIS signature exists (CHKP10) and would support a separate `model: standard` edge rather than a change to this one.
pages.statement: The [[shortest-integer-solution|SIS]] assumption implies [[digital-signature|DS]] in the random oracle model: a GPV signature on $\mu$ is a short $\mathbf{z}$ with $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{z} = H(\mu) \bmod q$, sampled from a discrete Gaussian using a short basis of $\Lambda_q^\perp(\mathbf{A})$, and the scheme is strongly unforgeable under chosen-message attack whenever $\mathbf{z} \mapsto \mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}$ is collision resistant on short inputs, which is SIS — [[GPV08 - Trapdoors for hard lattices and new cryptographic constructions|GPV08]].
pages.sketch: Trapdoor-sampled preimages have the same distribution as a discrete Gaussian conditioned on its image, so the reduction, holding a challenge $\mathbf{A}$ without a trapdoor, answers each hash query by sampling $\mathbf{z}$ first and programming $H(\mu) := \mathbf{A}\mathbf{z}$, and answers signing queries with those $\mathbf{z}$. A forgery $\mathbf{z}^*$ on $\mu^*$ differs from the reduction's own preimage $\mathbf{z}'$ of $H(\mu^*)$ except with negligible probability (preimage min-entropy), and $\mathbf{z}^* - \mathbf{z}'$ is a short nonzero SIS solution for $\mathbf{A}$.
pages.improvements_text:
- Signatures from SIS in the ROM without a lattice trapdoor, via Fiat-Shamir with aborts and rejection sampling — [[Lyu12 - Lattice Signatures Without Trapdoors|Lyu12]].
- Stateless hash-and-sign signatures from SIS in the standard model, via bonsai-tree basis delegation — [[CHKP10 - Bonsai Trees, or How to Delegate a Lattice Basis|CHKP10]].
